cognate: Gk κλέος = Ved. śrávas- (*ḱléwos); Gk (κατα)τίθημι = Ved. dhā- (*dʰeh₁-, both reduplicated presents τίθημι/dádhāti); Gk μέγας/μέγα = Ved. máh-/máhi (*méǵh₂). Three-word cognate match in Hdt 9.78.2 ~ RV 1.79.4c.
drift_or_renewal: Epithet slot: 'great' is kept cognate on both sides (μέγιστον, μέγα ~ máhi). Where Vedic has ákṣiti śrávaḥ with middle dhā- (RV 1.40.4b, 8.103.5b, 9.66.7c dhatte/dádhānaḥ ákṣiti śrávaḥ), Greek with κλέος + middle (κατα)θέσθαι shows renewed 'imperishable' epithets: ἀθάνατον (Plato Symp. 208c), ἄσβεστον (Simonides), while the cognate ἄφθιτον survives with κλέος only in Homer without the verb (Il. 9.413). Herodotus moves the formula into prose with the compound κατα-.
shared_syntax: Transitive *dʰeh₁- 'place, establish' with *ḱléwos as direct object and an adjective 'great' agreeing with it: κλέος καταθέσθαι μέγιστον ~ dhehi máhi śrávaḥ. Middle voice 'establish fame for oneself' on both sides: καταθέσθαι (aor. mid.) ~ dhatte, dádhānaḥ (mid.); active/causative 'place fame on someone' with god as agent: θεὸς παρέδωκε ... καταθέσθαι ~ asmé dhehi (2sg impv. addressed to Agni). In Od. 2.125 μέγα κλέος is object of middle ποιεῖται (τιθεῖσι there governs νόον, so it witnesses the adjective-noun pair, not the verb).
context: Hdt 9.78.2: Lampon tells Pausanias that a god has granted him, having saved Hellas, to lay up the greatest fame of all Greeks. RV 1.79.4c: prayer to Agni Jātavedas 'place great fame in us'. RV 1.40.4b: the giver of wealth to the priest 'establishes for himself imperishable fame'. Both are about fame as a durable deposit set up for a man, with the gods as granters: the same ideology, not a passing use of 'fame'. Counts: śrávas- + dhā- in 25 RV pādas, śrávas- + máh- in 17; κλέος + μέγας in 13 Homeric lines; κλέος + (κατα)τίθημι recurs in Herodotus (twice), Plato, Simonides. Fame + 'place' is not a necessary collocation in either language (Homer prefers κλέος ἄρνυμαι, ἔχω, ἔσται), so the shared verb is diagnostic.
phrase: *ḱléwos méǵh₂ dʰeh₁- 'establish great fame' (middle: 'for oneself'), beside *ḱléwos n̥dʰgʷʰitom

cognate: Gk εὐρύς = Ved. urú- (*h₁wérHus 'wide'); Gk πόντος = Ved. pánthā-/path- (*póntoh₁s, *pn̥th₁-).
drift_or_renewal: Drift on the noun: *póntoh₁s 'path, passage' stays 'path' in Vedic but is 'sea' in Greek; the adjective is the exact cognate in the same slot. The Greek uses keep the travel sense of the old 'path': one sails over/crosses the wide πόντος (ἐπιπλώς, περήσαμεν, ἐπέπλων εὐρέα πόντον), i.e. the sea is the wide passage.
shared_syntax: Attributive adjective + noun in agreement, both orders, and the same locatival case: Ved. uraú pathí (loc.), Gk εὐρέϊ πόντῳ (dat.-loc., 'on the wide sea'); also acc. of the way traversed: Ved. urúm ... pánthām ~ Gk εὐρέα πόντον; instr. pathā́ urúṇā 'by the wide path'.
context: RV: the wide path along which gods, the chariot or the sacrificial gift travel (8.68.13b urúm ráthāya pánthām; 10.107.1d urúḥ pánthāḥ dákṣiṇāyāḥ; 4.26.5b the falcon released 'by the wide path'; 3.54.9d gods standing on the wide path). Greek: the wide sea as the expanse travelled by ships (Homer, Hesiod) or by waves (Soph. Trach. 113). Formulaic on both sides: 4 RV pādas with urú- qualifying pánthā-, 9 Homeric lines, 3 more in Hesiod/h.Ap.; Sophocles inherits the epic phrase. 'Wide' + 'path/way' is a natural pairing, which keeps this at medium; what argues for inheritance is that Greek keeps the cognate adjective on the one noun that continues the 'path' word, and in the same travel frame (crossing, sailing over), i.e. an old 'wide path' collocation whose noun was reinterpreted as the sea-way.
phrase: *h₁wérus póntoh₁s 'the wide path' → Gk εὐρὺς πόντος 'the wide sea'
